title: Visual Neglect Laboratory
summary: Line bisection, cancellation and copying a scene, run on five fictional profiles: no difficulty, left neglect organised around the viewer, left neglect organised around each object, left visual field loss without neglect, and both together. An examiner prompt can be switched on and off. The copying task separates neglect from field loss cleanly, and separates the two kinds of neglect from each other.
learningObjectives: Explain why unilateral neglect is not blindness on one side.
Name the task signatures that separate neglect from visual field loss, including the opposite directions of the bisection error.
Distinguish neglect organised around the viewer from neglect organised around each object.
Explain what an examiner prompt does and does not fix, and why.
Say why neglect cannot be assigned to one brain region.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it. Nobody is tested and nothing here can assess anybody.
accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox and button controls; the drawings are display-only and nothing has to be clicked or dragged inside them. Each drawing is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a readout giving the headline result, the prompt state and the unprompted-to-prompted change, plus two tables: one breaking the current result down by line, by third of the page or by object in the scene, and one giving every profile's result on the current task with and without the prompt. Nothing carries meaning by colour: a bisection mark is a tall stroke and the true middle a short notch, a found star carries a stroke through it while a missed one does not, and an omitted part of a copy is simply absent. Every change announces a full summary through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Neglect against field loss, and viewer-centred against object-centred neglect: the task signatures that separate them and what cueing fixes
simulationNotes: Five fictional profiles, each a rule rather than a person, and three original tasks. Bisection deviation is a fraction of line length, positive rightward: viewer-centred neglect uses 0.06 plus 0.16 times one minus the line's position across the page, so the error grows for lines further left; object-centred neglect uses a constant 0.13 wherever the line sits; field loss uses a constant minus 0.05, towards the blind side. Cancellation uses a logistic in horizontal position drawn against a fixed seed (mulberry32, seed 20260807), with a steep function at the page edge for field loss rather than a gradient. Copying drops parts by page position for viewer-centred neglect and by side-within-object for object-centred neglect. The prompt multiplies the neglect component by 0.55, moves the viewer-centred copy cut-off leftwards, removes the field-loss effect entirely, and does nothing at all to object-centred copying because it is an instruction about the page. Reference values at the default settings - bisection means: no difficulty plus 0.3 per cent, viewer-centred neglect plus 14.0 per cent (18.4, 14.0 and 9.6 across the three lines), object-centred neglect plus 13.0 per cent on every line, field loss minus 5.0 per cent, both plus 8.9 per cent. Cancellation out of 26, unprompted then prompted: 26 and 26, 15 and 18, 19 and 24, 24 and 26, 14 and 18. Copying out of 19: 19 and 19, 10 and 13, 12 and 12, 19 and 19, 10 and 13. No clinical instrument is reproduced, no scoring is clinical, no real person is described, and nothing here diagnoses, assesses or gives a prognosis for anybody.
